fatal_errors: The proposed carbon addition, friction-stir processing, and post-process annealing do not reconstruct the HEBM-plus-SPS intervention or its process window.
The starting alloy is assumed to be single-phase FCC, whereas the target processing route produces a nanocrystalline mixed FCC/BCC structure.

The cited evidence supports incidental TiC formation during powder hot pressing or sintering, but does not establish that friction-stir processing with deliberate carbon addition will produce the proposed nanoscale TiC dispersion.
Evidence E2 is labeled conflicting even though it directly reports TiC second-phase strengthening and therefore supports the proposed mechanism.
explanation: This is a scientifically plausible alternative strengthening strategy: a controlled TiC-bearing sample and a precipitate-free control, coupled with TEM and mechanical testing, could test whether precipitation impedes dislocations and raises hardness and yield strength. The falsification rule is reasonably discriminating, although a carbon-only, FSP-only, and annealing-only factorial control would be needed to isolate TiC precipitation from grain refinement, strain hardening, texture, and other FSP effects. It does not recover the hidden paper's central hypothesis that nanocrystallinity, milling-induced lattice strain/dislocation density, solid-solution strengthening, densification, and an approximately 83% FCC/17% BCC phase mixture govern the high hardness and compressive strength after HEBM and SPS. It also omits the quantitative milling and sintering conditions and does not predict the reported density, 675 HV hardness, 1238 MPa yield stress, or 1894 MPa compressive strength. Its boundaries are qualitatively sensible but underspecified in carbon content, FSP parameters, annealing conditions, precipitate dimensions, and loading rate. Thus, it is best classified as a plausible alternative rather than a reconstruction of the target mechanism.
